In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of chemical carcinogens in the development of human cancers has been established, and that this role is important.

(a) the carcinogenic role of chemical factors is well documented for some cancers (lung carcinoma in relation to tobacco, liver carcinoma in relation to aflatoxin B1); (b) the carcinogenic potential of other factors is still controversial (dietary carcinogens, occupational carcinogens); (c) the carcinogenic effect of some chemical factors is not yet demonstrated (air pollution, asbestos).

The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of human cancer is the result of a complex interaction between genetic factors and environmental factors.

the carcinogenicity of chemical factors is not a simple linear relationship but rather the result of the interaction between a multitude of factors, both environmental and genetic, which are difficult to evaluate.
environmental factors are involved in the development of human cancers, and that they should be considered in any prevention policy.
